issues.legal_issue: An urban land ceiling law that limits excess vacant holdings and distributes acquired land to prevent concentration and promote equitable distribution advances the directive principles concerning community resources and concentration of wealth.
material_facts: The law imposed ceilings on vacant urban land and provided for acquisition of holdings above those ceilings.
Its stated scheme sought to prevent concentration of urban land and to distribute land equitably for the common good.
issues.conclusion: The law furthered the objectives of Article 39(b) and (c) and was protected by Article 31-C as it stood before the Forty-second Amendment, except for the invalid restriction on transfers of certain property within the ceiling area.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 39(b) and (c) direct equitable distribution of material resources to subserve the common good and prevention of concentration of wealth and means of production. The Court applied Article 31-C as it stood before the Forty-second Amendment and the framework stated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala and Waman Rao v. Union of India: where a post-1973 Ninth Schedule enactment is protected by Article 31-C, a challenge to its inclusion based on the protected fundamental-right provisions becomes otiose.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_urban_land_c: A litigant challenges the constitutionality of a law that imposes ceilings on vacant urban land.
predicates.law_limits_excess_urban_vacant_land: The law restricts holdings of vacant urban land above specified limits and provides for acquisition of excess land.
predicates.law_scheme_targets_concentration_and_equ: The law's scheme aims to prevent concentration of urban land and distribute it equitably for the common good.

issues.definition: When a challenged urban land ceiling law limits excess holdings and is designed to prevent concentration through equitable distribution, the law advances the stated distribution objectives and receives the stated constitutional protection.

issues.legal_issue: Defining a family for an urban land ceiling as an individual, that individual's spouse, and their unmarried minor children is not, by itself, an unconstitutional or arbitrary classification.
material_facts: The law defined a family as an individual, the individual's spouse, and their unmarried minor children.
The challenge asserted that this definition excluded adult children and joint families and could produce different permitted holdings.
The Court considered that the definition reflected the nuclear family increasingly prevalent in urban life and did not inevitably cause concentration of wealth.
issues.conclusion: The family definition was valid and did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a family definition merely because it excludes adult children or joint-family arrangements. The majority considered the definition in the context of contemporary urban family patterns and the law's distributive purpose under Article 39(b) and (c). Justice Sen also relied on the Court's prior approval of substantially similar family definitions in agrarian ceiling laws and referred to Union of India v. Valluri Basavaiah Chowdhary concerning legislative difficulties in imposing an urban ceiling.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_family_unit_: A litigant challenges the constitutional validity of the family unit used to calculate a land ceiling.
predicates.law_counts_individual_spouse_and_unmarri: The law treats an individual, their spouse, and their unmarried minor children as a single family unit.
predicates.definition_does_not_inevitably_concentra: The definition does not by itself or inevitably produce concentration of wealth contrary to the law's distributive purpose.

issues.definition: A challenged family unit consisting of an individual, spouse, and unmarried minor children is not unconstitutional where that definition does not inevitably cause wealth concentration.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory power to allot acquired excess vacant land for industrial or related purposes is valid when the governing standard requires disposal to serve the common good.
material_facts: The law authorized the State to allot acquired excess vacant land for purposes connected with industry and for housing industry employees.
The statutory definition of industry was broad, but the law also directed that acquired land be disposed of to subserve the common good.
The Court treated the allotment power as enabling rather than compulsory and held that each allotment had to serve the common good.
issues.conclusion: The disposal provision was valid when read as requiring every allotment, including one to an industry, to subserve the common good; a disposal that did not do so could be struck down.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 39(b) and (c), the Act's preamble, and the common-good direction govern disposal of acquired land. The broad language authorizing allotments must be read in that constitutional and statutory context. A private allotment may be permissible if it serves the common good, but land may not be acquired or allotted for a merely private purpose. The Court endorsed reading broad statutory language down to its lawful scope and retained judicial review of misuse or mala fide exercise of power.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_excess_land_: A litigant challenges the constitutionality of a statutory scheme for disposing of acquired excess vacant land.
predicates.law_authorizes_industrial_or_related_all: The law permits the government to allot acquired excess land for industrial purposes or related employee housing.
predicates.law_requires_disposal_to_serve_common_go: The law makes service of the common good the governing standard for disposal of acquired land.

issues.definition: A challenged disposal scheme permitting industrial or related allotments is valid only if each disposal serves the common good.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory maximum amount payable for acquired excess vacant land is valid when the amount is not illusory or confiscatory.
material_facts: The law set principles for calculating the amount payable for acquired excess vacant land and imposed a maximum payable in any case.
The maximum could be lower than the market value of a large holding, but the Court considered the prescribed amount substantial rather than fictitious or nominal.
issues.conclusion: The maximum amount provision was valid and was neither illusory nor confiscatory.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as altered by the Twenty-fifth Amendment, permits an amount to be fixed by law and bars a challenge merely that the amount is inadequate; the amount must not be illusory. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd., and State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy, and considered the maximum amount substantial in light of the social context. Justice Iyer also reasoned that a ceiling on the maximum is not discriminatory unless the maximum itself is a hoax or trivial.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A litigant challenges a legal maximum on payment for property acquired by the State.
predicates.law_sets_a_maximum_payment_for_acquired_: The law fixes a maximum amount payable for property acquired under it, even where the property's value may exceed that maximum.
predicates.maximum_payment_is_substantial_rather_th: The maximum amount is more than a fictitious or merely nominal payment.

issues.definition: A challenged payment cap is valid and not confiscatory when the law sets a maximum for acquired property and that maximum is substantial rather than illusory.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction requiring permission to transfer built-up urban property within the permitted ceiling area is invalid.
material_facts: The law required prior written permission for transfers of urban or urbanisable land with a building, or part of a building, including property within the ceiling area.
The permission power lacked adequate legislative guidelines governing when permission should be granted or refused.
The restriction applied even to property that the law otherwise left within the holder's permitted ceiling.
issues.conclusion: The transfer restriction was invalid insofar as it applied to urban or urbanisable land with a building, or a portion of a building, within the ceiling area.
issues.legal_principle: At the relevant time, Article 19(1)(f) protected the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property, subject to reasonable restrictions. A restriction on transfer of built-up property within the permitted ceiling was outside the measure's proper scope and was unsupported by adequate guidelines controlling the decision-maker's discretion. Justice Sen relied on the reasoning in Excel Wear v. Union of India concerning the scope of a guaranteed right and its correlative freedoms.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_tra: A litigant challenges a legal restriction on transferring urban property.
predicates.built_property_is_within_permitted_ceili: The property being transferred is urban or urbanisable land with a building, or part of a building, within the permitted ceiling area.
predicates.transfer_requires_permission_without_ade: The law requires prior permission for the transfer and does not adequately guide the authority's decision to grant or refuse it.

issues.definition: A permission-based transfer restriction is invalid when it applies to built property within the permitted ceiling and lacks adequate guidelines.
